Who these notes are for

These notes support Edexcel GCSE Physics students applying series and parallel rules, interpreting component graphs and planning circuit investigations.

Sixteen teaching sections contain diagrams, core concepts, worked calculations and numbered exercise sets with subquestions. Four pages of solutions provide marking points and explanation guidance. Current, Potential Difference & Resistance is a useful starting point if the foundations need practice.

20 pages · 16 exercise sets · Solutions with marking points

Topics covered

  • Current, voltage and resistance in series and parallel
  • Independent switching, circuit design and meter connections
  • I-V graphs for fixed resistors, filament lamps and diodes
  • LDRs and NTC thermistors
  • Collecting readings, plotting graphs and investigating sensors
  • Comparing combined resistance at controlled voltage and temperature
  • Random variation, zero errors, meter loading and safe practical work

A focused circuit handout, not a complete GCSE course. Independent Study with Dr material, not an official Pearson Edexcel publication or examination mark scheme. Existing source and diagram credits are retained. Practical activities require suitable low-voltage equipment and teacher-approved methods.

Key ideas at a glance

Apply the correct circuit rule

In series, steady current is the same throughout, voltages add and resistances add. In parallel, each branch has the same voltage and branch currents add. For positive resistances, the combined parallel resistance is below the smallest branch resistance.

Use the axes when interpreting I-V graphs

For current on the vertical axis and voltage on the horizontal axis, a steeper straight ohmic-resistor line means lower resistance. For a curved graph, use R = V/I at the chosen operating point rather than treating a tangent gradient as 1/R.

Control conditions and evaluate measurements

Keep fixed-resistor temperatures approximately constant when comparing resistance. Repeat readings to reduce random variation; repeating does not remove a persistent zero offset. Measure voltage across the whole arrangement and total current when calculating combined resistance.
